items.title: Suit alleges Louisiana land deal between SpaceX and ExxonMobil violates open meetings law
items.summary: Suit says parish board was manipulated to allow deal to go through and settlement agreement hidden from public After ending a lawsuit over ExxonMobil ’s damage to wetlands, Louisiana officials moved quickly to approve a deal giving SpaceX access to 125,000 acres (50,600 hectares) of marsh formerly owned by the oil company. A new lawsuit now alleges they did so in violation of the state’s open meetings law. The lawsuit, filed by three south-central Louisiana residents, follows state and Vermilion parish officials’ approval of what is estimated to be a record $27.5bn tax incentive package for SpaceX’s Starbase Louisiana project, announced over the summer . The officials violated the state’s open meetings law eight times while facilitating the agreement in attempts to “keep the public in the dark about what they are doing for SpaceX”, the lawsuit alleges.

items.originalTitle: You Can’t Cast Your Family
items.author: Heidi Levitt
items.title: You Can’t Cast Your Family
items.summary: Chevy Chase in a scene from the 1989 film "Christmas Vacation." —Warner Brothers—Getty Images One of the first films I cast was the holiday classic National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation . I was one lucky 27-year-old when my bosses invited me to partner with them and help complete casting the Griswold family. In those days, we auditioned scores of actors in person. Almost everyone came through our doors to read for their roles, something now mostly done over Zoom or by offer only. In my humble opinion, casting has taken a nosedive because we've lost that intimate experience of sitting face-to-face, listening, observing, and discovering a character together. Sometimes it took several auditions, chemistry reads, callbacks, and director work sessions to get it right. We had to slow down and really see the person sitting across from us. Every holiday season, when millions of American families gather around their Thanksgiving and Christmas tables, I think about those wacky Griswold family dynamics. The relatives who arrive uninvited. The holiday disasters. The misunderstandings, the arguments, and the love beneath all the madness. In my husband Charlie's family, Thanksgiving was a beloved tradition. His parents divorced when he was 15, and the family learned to move between households and maintain a certain equilibrium. Everyone found ways to come together, but rarely did anyone dig deeper into what was happening beneath the surface. The family had learned to adapt and to compartmentalize their feelings. Thanksgiving 2019, in Charlie's hometown of Washington, D.C., should have been different. Charlie's mom had passed away years earlier, and a couple of months before traveling east, we had told his dad, stepmother, and siblings that Charlie, at just 57, had been diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer's disease and was leaving his job as an art director at UCLA Magazine. But once we arrived, the diagnosis seemed to be swept under the rug. Charlie looked so well. His Alzheimer's was invisible to them. I remember worrying about a fancy dinner at the Cosmos Club because Charlie needed to wear a tie, and neither of us could quite manage to tie one. A small thing, perhaps, but one of those early signs of struggle. What his family might have noticed were the changes already taking place in our marriage. Charlie's short temper and his uncertainty about what kind of work he might pursue next. My super-sensitive artist husband had actually been the one to recognize that something was wrong and asked to see a doctor. I had simply hoped his mood would change and that further tests might reveal something else. We were on a kind of autopilot in those early days, and I was just beginning to realize there was little I could do to solve this problem. As always, I had my camera with me. I filmed the family around the Thanksgiving table, sharing the things they were grateful for. Looking back at that footage now is painful. Charlie's father, a distinguished writer and scholar who had spent nearly 50 years at a Washington think tank after serving in the White House, beamed with pride at his two sons, his beloved wife, stepchildren, and the grandchildren who made him so happy. He was finishing his final memoir and remained intellectually engaged with the world. Yet his oldest son's Alzheimer's diagnosis never entered the Thanksgiving conversation. Charlie himself was still hopeful about his next act. He was making art, walking the streets of Los Angeles with his camera, and building a website, walkingnla.com, to document his discoveries. His words were beginning to falter, but his wit, his agency, and his joie de vivre remained intact. "Everybody gets something," he would say, accepting his diagnosis with a kind of courage and wry humor that I still marvel at. He certainly wasn't looking for a pity party. He wanted to enjoy his family, and perhaps for a few hours forget what was happening to him. But somewhere between respecting Charlie's wishes and avoiding the uncomfortable truth, we all managed to sidestep the elephant at the Thanksgiving table. I was part of that conceit, too. Perhaps that Thanksgiving we were all too frightened of what we didn't know. Fear of the unknown has a funny way of disguising itself as good manners. When COVID arrived, our world grew smaller. Uncertain about what either of us could do for work, I decided I needed to make a film, WALK WITH ME . Documenting four years of our lives became my way of coping, and a way to give Charlie purpose. I convinced my family to participate because our story belonged to millions of other families like ours, and that the film could confront the stigma and shame surrounding Alzheimer's disease. What I hadn't anticipated was that it would also document my own transformation into a caregiver. At the time, caregiving wasn't even in my vocabulary. I will always be grateful for the quiet conversations we had during that time. Making our documentary meant asking my family to bear witness on camera to some of the most difficult moments of our lives. It took years for all of us to work through what that meant. And it took me even longer to own up to adding "caregiver" to my identity. Watching that 2019 Thanksgiving footage now, I see a family functioning beautifully on the surface. But I wish I had asked the questions we were all avoiding. What would happen when Charlie could no longer manage everyday tasks? Who would help? How would we pay for that help? What would happen to my work, our marriage, and our independence? I wish I had understood sooner that living with a progressive disease meant grieving each loss while constantly readjusting and improvising so Charlie could remain in the lane of "normal." Today, I choose restaurants with quiet tables. In movie theaters, I sit beside him in an aisle seat near the exit in case the film becomes too loud or intense and we need to leave. Before flying, I find out where the family bathrooms are located at the airport. I have to pre-think and map out nearly every adventure because I still want Charlie to be with me, and I still want our lives to feel "normal." But the truth is, nothing is normal anymore. And I wish I had brought his family and friends into the conversation earlier rather than trying to manage so much of it myself. Perhaps if I'd spoken more openly about my fears, they would have understood sooner how much we needed them. Perhaps they would have prioritized showing up for Charlie, and for me. I can't know that. I was still struggling to understand what was happening myself. It took me nearly two years to confront Charlie's father and tell him how hurt I was that he continued to speak as though nothing was happening. I suspected he was afraid to acknowledge the changes in his son. What parent wants to imagine losing a child, even gradually, to a disease that steals so much? Seven years later, Charlie needs help with nearly every activity of daily living. I have become his caregiver, his advocate, his interpreter, and often his compass in a world that has become increasingly difficult for him to navigate. Our children have had to learn how to remain connected to a father who can no longer communicate as he once did. And I have learned that love, however deep, cannot replace the practical, emotional, and financial support that caregiving requires. This holiday season, millions of Americans will brave crowded highways and impossible airports to gather with relatives they may not have seen for months. And somewhere between the turkey, the football games, and the arguments about politics, someone may notice that something feels a little off. Grandma tells the same story three times. An uncle who was always the life of the party becomes irritated when the conversation gets too loud. Mom, who once managed the entire holiday dinner, now seems overwhelmed by the simplest preparations. It's easy to dismiss these changes as aging, stress, exhaustion, or eccentricity. Sometimes that's exactly what they are. Not every forgotten word or strange behavior signals dementia. But sometimes something more serious is happening, and the holiday table may be the first place everyone has an opportunity to see it. This holiday season, perhaps the greatest gift we can give the people we love is our attention. Put down the phone. Listen. Observe. Ask questions. And when something is changing, don't stop at acknowledging it. Have the awkward conversations about what care will require, who will provide it, how you'll pay for it, and how you'll show up for one another when things become more difficult. And please, don't stand on ceremony. Sometimes love requires a little less politeness and a lot more persistence. Which brings me back to the Griswolds. They never managed a perfect vacation or holiday, but boy, did they hang on tight. I loved helping cast that motley crew, and I suspect every actor brought a little of their own family lore to those gloriously ridiculous performances. The thing about casting is that you spend a great deal of time looking for the right person for the right role. Of course, you can't cast your own family. You don't get to choose who shows up, who disappoints you, or who rises magnificently to the occasion. But you can ask people to pay closer attention and take on a bigger role. You can insist that the family gather around the table not simply to give thanks, but to really see one another. And when it comes to caring for the people we love, I think we need to stop being so afraid of making a scene. After all, you may not be able to cast your own family. But you can demand a callback.

items.originalTitle: Connection Must Be More Than a Holiday Tradition
items.author: Suzanne McCormick
items.title: Connection Must Be More Than a Holiday Tradition
items.summary: —skynesher—Getty Images It’s Thanksgiving Day. For many of us, this means turkey and stuffing in the oven. Football playing in the background. Family and friends gathering to share a meal . And someone asking: “How about we go around and say what we’re thankful for?” People share stories, discuss milestones, maybe even acknowledge personal challenges. And before it’s time for pumpkin pie, we’ve learned something new about one another and feel more connected than before. Unfortunately, experiences of connection like this happen too infrequently. Today, loneliness and social isolation are among the most pressing public health challenges facing our country. According to a new Social Connection in America™ survey , 40% of Americans report moderate to severe loneliness. Nearly 70% get together with others no more than once or twice a month. While connecting virtually is a routine part of daily life for many, only 24% of people say it is as satisfying as spending time together in person. As a leader at the YMCA, I spend a lot of time thinking about connection and community, and what happens when people don’t have either. The consequences are real and extend beyond feeling down or lonely. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), a lack of social connection is associated with an increased risk of heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, dementia, earlier death, and other serious health conditions. In 2023, then-U.S. Surgeon General Dr. Vivek Murthy warned that the nation’s epidemic of loneliness and isolation poses serious risks to both individual and public health. These troubling trends and consequences coincide with a retreat from public life. A 2025 report from the Survey Center on American Life found that Americans began spending substantially less time in “t hird places ” outside of the home and school or work—such as YMCAs, parks, and houses of worship—after the pandemic and still have not fully returned. A range of factors appear to be contributing to this decline, from the rise of remote work and the growing amount of time people are spending online, to stubbornly high inflation and the resulting increased cost of living. Americans are staying home more and going out and socializing less. When we spend less time in shared spaces, we lose natural opportunities to connect with others. Connection becomes something we have to intentionally seek out, rather than something woven throughout our day. The good news is that spaces for connection are all around us. The challenge for each of us is to step into those spaces, open ourselves up to new relationships, and prioritize our intrinsic need for human connection. In 1851, 175 years ago this December, the first YMCA was established in the United States. It was founded by Thomas Valentine Sullivan, a sea captain and missionary looking to provide a safe “home away from home” for sailors and merchants in need of community and support. As the needs of communities evolved, so did the Y. Our programs have changed and expanded over time, but creating places where people can find support and connection has remained central to our work. Today, third spaces continue to provide that same community and support people need to thrive. They foster a deep sense of belonging and shared purpose—and often among people whose paths might not cross otherwise. Over time, a familiar face turns into a friendship, a class becomes a community, and a third space feels like a second home. We know the ingredients for connection—programs that invite contribution, spaces that encourage conversation, staff trained to welcome—and how they fit together to create opportunities for growth, relationships, and belonging. It can be hard to find the time, resources, or even courage to try something new, but the benefits of connection are worth it. This Thanksgiving, I hope we’ll all take time to appreciate the people around us. I hope we’ll listen a little more closely to their stories, share a little more of our own, and reflect on how meaningful it feels to truly connect with another person. And I hope that after the dishes are cleared and everyone goes home, we’ll continue to make the effort. Because we need connection, and we need it to be more than a holiday tradition.

items.originalTitle: The Most Shocking Moments of the Hunting Wives Season 2 Finale, Ranked
items.author: Barry Levitt
items.title: The Most Shocking Moments of the Hunting Wives Season 2 Finale, Ranked
items.summary: Malin Akerman in The Hunting Wives Season 2 —Courtesy of Netflix The Hunting Wives knows how to bring the drama. The series, created by Rebecca Cutter based on the novel by May Cobb, became a surprise smash hit for Netflix last year. The show follows the lives of a group of women in the fictional town of Maple Brook, Texas, a world overflowing with sex, deceit, and—you guessed it— murder . Season 2 of The Hunting Wives delivers a new series of challenges for Sophie ( Brittany Snow ), Margo (Malin Åkerman), and Callie (Jamie Ray Newman), as the murders from Season 1 continue to hang over Maple Brook. Things come to a head in a finale filled with twists, and we’ve broken down all the biggest revelations below, ranking them from least to most jaw-dropping. 6. A marriage no more Evan Jonigkeit and Brittany Snow —Courtesy of Netflix As Sophie gets closer to Margo, she’s pulled further and further from Graham (Evan Jonigkeit), her estranged husband. At the beginning of the season, Sophie appeared keen to rehabilitate their marriage, and even started couples counselling. But in falling head-over-heels in love with Margo, she’s left Graham completely, and they’ve agreed to divorce. In the finale, Graham has a big surprise for Sophie. He’s filing for full custody of their son and wants to take him back to Boston, effectively erasing her from their lives. It’s not an earth-shattering surprise given how distant Sophie has been from Graham and her son this season, but Graham’s decision has enormous implications for Sophie, putting her in a desperate situation. It also confirms for Sophie that there’s no going back to the way things once were. 5. A police case is finally closed Karen Rodriguez and Branton Box —Courtesy of Netflix Deputy Wanda Salazar (Karen Rodriguez) has worked tirelessly to solve the murder of Margo’s brother Kyle (Michael Aaron Milligan). In the finale, she finally uncovers undeniable evidence that Margo killed Abby. When Sophie and Margo were held at gunpoint earlier in the season, Margo secretly called 9-1-1 and never hung up the phone, so Sophie’s confession to Margo after the shootout was recorded, and Salazar has the recording. This also leads Salazar and Sheriff Jonny (Branton Box) to connect Sophie killing Kyle to Margo killing Abby, as they realize the pair are protecting each other from the law. Finally, they’ve solved everything. Yet it all comes crashing down. Jonny goes to Jed and Margo’s house to question Margo, but Margo isn’t home. Instead, Jed tells Jonny about his presidential endorsement and tells him that in exchange for closing the case and leaving the past in the past, he’ll make Jonny a ranger when he becomes governor. Jonny doesn’t hesitate to take the offer, devastating Salazar. This keeps both Margo and Sophie out of jail, and reminds us of the endlessly corrupting properties of power. 4. Nadia's fate Kim Matula as Nadia —Courtesy of Netflix Nadia (Kim Matula) has proven to be one of the most exciting new additions in Season 2. She’s arrived in Maple Brook to film a Real Housewives -style docuseries starring Callie and Margo, but the series has an ulterior motive: it’s actually a true-crime show meant to uncover the truth behind Abby’s death, the murder that informed much of Season 1. Nadia has finally figured out what the audience knows: it was Margo who killed Abby. But before Nadia has a chance to present the evidence, she gets into a fatal crash while pursuing Sophie and Margo. This reveals that it was Nadia who was chasing the duo in the penultimate episode cliffhanger, and not someone hired by Margo’s husband Jed (Dermot Mulroney). Nadia’s black SUV flips over multiple times. She crawls out and sees a shocked Sophie and Margo standing over her. Her vehicle's OnStar support system tries to make contact with her, but the ladies cover her mouth instead of helping her, and Nadia dies. It’s likely that the crash would have killed Nadia anyway, but it’s hard to deny that Sophie and Margo speed things along. It remains to be seen whether this decision will come back to haunt them, but it’s a genuinely shocking reveal that Nadia was the one in that car. Though it’s not entirely surprising that she dies in the finale (she was trying to take down our leads, after all), the circumstances behind her demise will certainly cause jaws to drop. 3. A major campaign announcement Malin Akerman and Dermot Mulroney in the season finale —Courtesy of Netflix Jed has been running for governor of Texas ever since The Hunting Wives began. In the Season 2 finale, a breakthrough arrives when he gets an endorsement from the President, which should go a long way in securing his victory. As the campaign ramps up, Jed has kept Margo under lock and key, keeping her monitored by security 24/7 to prevent her from seeing Sophie, or pursuing any other extramarital dalliances. The ever-determined Sophie gets to Margo anyway, and when Margo tells her about the news of the endorsement, she hatches a plan. Sophie wants Margo to admit her abortion live on air at Jed’s press conference. It’s her hope that this would expose the complete hypocrisy of his campaign, shattering her husband's hard-right conservative push for family values and exposing it all as fraudulent. One of the key principles of Jed’s campaign was that abortion was tantamount to murder, so revealing that his own wife had an abortion because of an affair could destroy him. Surprisingly, Margo agrees, because while this will devastate her marriage, it also means that she and Sophie can be together. When the press conference arrives, Margo reveals her abortion. Except instead of using it against Jed, she uses it as an opportunity to bolster support for him. She weaponizes the story, turning it into a moment of repentance, which impresses the press. Jed’s team is immediately struck by how well it plays. It does mean one thing, however: Margo and Sophie’s relationship is officially over. This is a genuinely massive revelation as Margo chooses Jed over Sophie in front of the entire world—but this is The Hunting Wives , and things are going to get even wilder. 2. A damning recording Snow and Akerman as Sophie and Margo —Courtesy of Netflix At the end of the Season 2 finale, Sophie confronts Margo over her betrayal at the press conference. Margo reveals that she made a deal with Jed, getting him to stop the police investigation so Sophie can walk free. They can never speak again, but otherwise Sophie would have been looking at a lifetime in jail. A devastated Sophie says, “You promised me you were coming back to me no matter what.” “You know me better than that,” Margo responds. Sophie is in big trouble. She’s without a job, and Margo wasn’t just the love of her life—she was her financial support. Now she’s lost both. Sophie does have a plan: she tells Margo she wants $10 million. We flash back to the Season 1 finale, but with a new revelation: back then, when Margo confessed to killing Abby, Sophie was recording on her phone. Margo is stunned, and she can’t hide that she’s impressed by Sophie’s forward thinking: “Clever girl,” she praises her. Sophie refuses to relent, threatening Margo that she has plenty of backups of the file. Margo agrees, but it means their relationship will never be the same again: Says Margo: “You cross this line, there’s no coming back.” “I know,” Sophie responds. 1. A time jump into the future By season's end, Sophie and Margo's future hangs in the balance —Courtesy of Netflix Sophie and Margo’s romance shattering for good somehow isn’t the biggest revelation in the Season 2 finale of The Hunting Wives . Because immediately after that confrontation, the show moves two years into the future. That’s a massive jump, given that Season 2 takes place mere weeks after the end of Season 1. In this flash forward, Sophie is looking remarkably glamorous, ordering an expensive drink at a bar, sporting a black AMEX card, the very same kind of card Margo used to spoil her with. On the news, she sees an announcement from Governor Jed Banks, passing a “Turn Away Gay” bill that allows medical professionals to deny care to LGBTQ Americans if it infringes on their religious beliefs. Margo, Jed’s bisexual wife, stands next to him smiling, infuriating Sophie. Then, she gets a call from someone too shocked to speak. She hears the breathing, and we see that it’s Margo, covered in blood. Before Margo can speak, the season ends. The moment is not dissimilar to the end of Season 1, when Sophie answers Kyle’s phone after killing him, unable to speak to Margo on the other line. Except now the roles are reversed, and we don’t know who Margo has killed. The most likely contender is Jed. Perhaps Margo has become a shell of herself after two years under Jed’s control, choosing who she sees and how she sees them. Maybe a bill that would explicitly prevent her from getting healthcare was the last straw, and she’s no longer able to play the political game. It could also be Callie, who hates Margo with a passion after she spurned her for Sophie. Callie also believes that Margo killed her newest lover Nadia, and is last seen in Season 2 shooting at a poster of Margo. Even more intriguing is the fact that Margo calls Sophie at all, after two years of presumably no contact. Margo told her that there’s no coming back, but in a moment of desperation, Sophie is the one she calls. It seems that their relationship is far from over. And with the show already renewed for a third season, hopefully it won’t be too long before all our burning questions are answered.
